title: batching-sla-slipback-mitigation-notes
content:
Incident summary:

Short: Between 2025-02-09 22:30 UTC and 2025-02-10 03:10 UTC we observed a progressive SLA slip on hosted inference endpoints using continuous batching. P50/P95 latency climbed ~2.3x and successful throughput dropped; token cost per request rose as batches collapsed to size=1 for large fraction of requests. Small subset (~3%) of pods started hitting transient OOMs that correlated with heavy KV cache churn.

Impact:
- Customer-facing API saw increased 500/504 errors and timeouts for model family `rw-instruct-*` on region us-west-2.
- Effective throughput down ~18% at peak; latency P95 increased from 420ms -> ~980ms.
- Internal alerting: high error-rate, pod restarts, and autoscaler flaps.

Quick timeline (UTC):
- 2025-02-09 22:24: first spike in single-request batches reported by metrics anomaly job (batch-size distribution shift).
- 2025-02-09 22:36: PagerDuty triggered (SRE primary).
- 2025-02-09 22:40: On-call triage: rolled collection of profiling traces and KV cache metrics.
- 2025-02-09 23:05: Identified high KV cache tombstone churn concurrent with a recent model variant rollout (PR #1497 merged earlier that day).
- 2025-02-09 23:28: Attempted safe mitigation: toggle-batching-to-conservative (feature flag) for affected model; partial improvement.
- 2025-02-10 00:10: Some pods started OOMing; rolled nodes to older node image as test.
- 2025-02-10 01:05: Full rollback of model variant (rollback of PR #1497) and restart of affected deployment completed.
- 2025-02-10 02:40: Batch size distribution and latency trending back toward baseline.
- 2025-02-10 03:10: All alerts silenced; incident declared resolved (monitoring continued).

Root-cause hypothesis (summary):
- The model variant change adjusted KV cache priming behavior and increased per-request KV auxiliary memory used during token generation when prefix hits are rare. That change interacts poorly with the continuous-batching heuristics: when KV warm-up delays exceed batching window, requests wait and then drop out of batched slots, causing many single-request batches. This both increases per-token work and increases memory pressure (stale KV entries + tombstone churn during pruning) leading to sporadic OOMs on a subset of pods.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Heatmaps of batch-size-by-time show sudden shift to batch=1 correlating with the rollout time.
- Heap profiles show a growing allocation class labeled `kv_aux_buffer` peaking on OOMing pods.
- KV cache metrics: tombstone-rate up ~5x during incident window; prune cycles triggered more often.
- Rolling back the variant reduced both tombstone-rate and batch collapse within 30–60 minutes.

Mitigations applied (ordered):
1) Immediate: set feature flag `continuous_batching_mode=conservative` for rw-instruct models in us-west-2. Command used: 
   - curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://console.internal/api/featureflags/toggle -d '{"flag":"continuous_batching_mode","value":"conservative","scope":"rw-instruct:us-west-2"}'
2) Restarted runtimes gracefully (kubectl rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime-rw) to force GC and free KV auxiliary allocations.
   - kubectl -n inference rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime-rw --selector=model-group=rw-instruct
3) Increased pod memory (temporary): bumped resource requests/limits + restarted to reduce OOM tail risk while rollback evaluated.
4) Rolled back model variant rollout (reverted PR #1497).

What worked:
- Conservative batching setting immediately reduced single-request batch percentage by ~60% and lowered P95.
- Rollback removed the underlying trigger for KV churn and stabilized memory metrics.

What didn’t help / false leads:
- Node image bump (kernel tuning) did not materially change tombstone churn rate.
- Draining pods one-by-one was slow; better to restart whole deployment for rapid GC in this case.

Short-term runbook additions (to include in on-call playbook):
- ADD: quick-check list when continuous-batching alert fires:
  1) Inspect batch-size histogram (last 15m) and token-per-request distribution.
  2) Check KV cache tombstone-rate and prune-frequency.
  3) Check recent model rollouts (git commits/PRs deployed in last 4h).
  4) Toggle continuous batching to `conservative` as first automated mitigation.
  5) If tombstone-rate high, consider `kv-prune-delay=short` (see caution below) or full rollback of variant.
- Add a runbook snippet with concrete commands for toggling flags and restarting: keep exact curl/kubectl examples above.

Longer-term engineering action items (owners & ETA):
- ENG-RUNTIME: Add telemetry to associate batch-ticket wait-time with batch-window eviction (Owner: Tom Nguyen, ETA: 2025-03-15).
- ENG-KV: Investigate tombstone lifecycle and add defensive caps on per-request kv_aux allocation; add soft-fail path to avoid OOM (Owner: Asha Patel, ETA: 2025-04-01).
- ENG-BATCHING: Modify batching heuristic to delay batch assignment until KV warm-up completes for high-KV models (Owner: Michael Li, ETA: 2025-05-01).
- SRE: Create a dashboard that surfaces model-variant rollout events tied to batching and KV metrics (Owner: Sara Kim, ETA: 2025-03-01).

On-call checklist (quick):
- Pager -> ack -> gather correlating telemetry (batch histogram, kv metrics, recent deploys).
- If batch collapse observed, immediately flip `continuous_batching_mode=conservative` for affected scopes.
- If tombstone-rate > 3x baseline and OOMs observed, escalate to ENG-KV and consider rolling back recent model variant.
- If rollbacks are needed, coordinate with Product/Model team (owner of PR) and schedule a canary rollback first, then global.

Post-incident notes / learning points:
- Continuous batching heuristics are brittle to model-side changes that change per-request KV behavior. We must treat batching and KV as coupled subsystems and test them jointly in pre-prod.
- Add a pre-deploy checklist item: run a KV-stress-local benchmark and batch-simulation workload for any variant touching kv priming code.
- The feature-flagging system saved us; ensure rollback playbooks are well-documented and accessible from on-call console.

Draft runbook snippet (to be added under Confluence / runbooks):
- Trigger: alert `batching_single_request_rate > 30%` OR `p95_latency_increase > 2x` for model group.
- Step 0: gather metrics (links to dashboard).
- Step 1: toggle batching to conservative: curl ... (see Mitigations above).
- Step 2: if no improvement in 15m, check `kv_tombstone_rate` -> if > 3x baseline, contact ENG-KV and consider rollback.
- Step 3: if pods OOMing, scale memory up temporarily and schedule a restart of the deployment.
- Step 4: After resolution, run retrospective and add findings to postmortem.

Open questions we still need to answer:
- Why did the model variant change increase kv_aux allocations per request? (Engineering to trace exact code paths.)
- Can we make KV cache pruning less aggressive without causing unbounded memory use?
- Is there a fast runtime mitigation that proactively stalls requests that would otherwise degrade batching (better backpressure)?

Immediate next steps assigned:
- Sara Kim: publish these notes and update on-call runbook fragment (ETA: 2025-02-18).
- Tom Nguyen: instrument batch-wait vs kv-warmup correlation metric (ETA: 2025-03-15).
- Asha Patel: prototype a soft-cap on kv_aux per-request and test in staging (ETA: 2025-03-22).
- Michael Li: propose batching heuristic patch to avoid premature batch release (PR draft by 2025-03-08).

Appendix (raw debugging snippets copied during on-call):
- Batch histogram query (promql): sum by(batch_size) (rate(serving_batch_assigned_total{model_group="rw-instruct"}[5m]))
- KV tombstone metric: rate(kv_cache_tombstones_total[1m])
- Restart command: kubectl -n inference rollout restart deployment/serving-runtime-rw --selector=model-group=rw-instruct
- Feature flag toggle (example): curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" https://console.internal/api/featureflags/toggle -d '{"flag":"continuous_batching_mode","value":"conservative","scope":"rw-instruct:us-west-2"}'

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Keep conservative mode as our escape hatch but don’t let it be default; it hurts overall throughput.
- Add automated playbook run in on-call Slack channel which will post suggested command snippets when the alert fires.
- Follow-up postmortem should include a short timeline with timestamps and graphs and be marked P2 since customer-visible but mitigated within hours.

End of draft.
